added_claims.speaker: Rich
added_claims.quote: They're all about crunching data, simulating, abstracting, creating models. But where they lack this ability to define self is they don't contextualize that within the greater environment.
added_claims.claim: AI models do only the abstract model-building (left-hemisphere) work and lack the feedback loop that checks models against the external environment, so they cannot recalibrate the way a brain does when misaligned (pain, fear).

added_claims.speaker: Niels
added_claims.quote: I don't know if it was Ken Griffin or Paul Tuda Jones it seemed like some of those guys who came out and saying well you know
added_claims.claim: Niels recalls well-known hedge fund managers (possibly Ken Griffin, Paul Tudor Jones) saying AI is far from producing alpha, with gains mainly in programming efficiency rather than alpha production.

added_claims.speaker: Niels
added_claims.quote: D A DT for markets. Don't ask, don't think.
added_claims.claim: Niels reports (his interpretation) that Saxo's former chief strategist links the current private credit debacle to a new market acronym, 'DADT': don't ask, don't think, i.e. investors avoid scrutinising credit risk.

added_claims.speaker: Niels
added_claims.quote: I think still people are more biased to looking at the oil price but it hasn't been doing anything for a long time despite all the challenges we've had in um in the Middle East.
added_claims.claim: Niels notes oil has been largely flat for a long time despite Middle East disruptions, even though most observers still anchor on the oil price rather than electricity as the growth input.
added_claims.testable: partly - oil price trend history is checkable

added_claims.speaker: Niels
added_claims.quote: further sanctions against a couple of oil companies in Russia and the oil prices is up uh quite sharply uh today 5% right now
added_claims.claim: A policy shock (new US sanctions on Russian oil companies) lifted crude about 5% intraday, an example of an exogenous event that can start an energy trend.

added_claims.speaker: Niels
added_claims.quote: Albeit uh there is more volatility in the uh returns from managers um at least when I see the ones I can see on a daily basis uh including our own uh for that matter.
added_claims.claim: Even in a constructive trend environment, CTA manager returns showed higher day-to-day volatility in late October 2025, linked to big precious metals swings that may mark a short-term top correction.
added_claims.indicator: manager daily return volatility; precious metals swings
added_claims.testable: partly - needs CTA index daily data

added_claims.speaker: Rich
added_claims.quote: but you just got to stick to the process.
added_claims.claim: After a poor first six months of 2025 Rich doubted whether the models still worked but argues the discipline is to stick to the process, and that deeper understanding of why trends occur raises his comfort with the methodology.
added_claims.testable: partly - adherence benefit can be tested vs rule-overriding

added_claims.speaker: Rich
added_claims.quote: you know the energies they're turning. They're going bullish. Um the the metals I think you know it might be a bit of a breather for them.
added_claims.claim: Rich: trend models were turning long in energies while metals might take a breather after their run, but systems remained active in metals (not over yet).
added_claims.indicator: trend model signals in energies and metals

added_claims.speaker: Niels
added_claims.quote: it was only a few years that really were difficult there were also plenty of good years
added_claims.claim: Caveat: trend following's post-GFC difficulty was limited to a few years (Niels recalls roughly 2018-2020; 2014 was strong), so it was not a decade-long failure.

added_claims.speaker: Rich
added_claims.quote: buying the dip syndrome I think was something of the past. I don't think buying the dip is going to continue going forward
added_claims.claim: Buy-the-dip was a behavioral phenomenon tied to the QE-era compression; with central banks decoupled and markets less correlated, Rich expects it to fade, which favours trends.
added_claims.conditions: depends on central banks staying uncoordinated
added_claims.testable: partly - dip-buying payoff and correlations measurable

added_claims.speaker: Niels
added_claims.quote: Let me just mention that the trend barometer yesterday finished at 52. So, that is a strong reading and uh it's coming up and uh supports uh what's going on
added_claims.claim: Niels uses the Trend Barometer (52, rising) as a gauge of how favourable the environment is for trend followers; 52 is read as a strong reading consistent with positive CTA returns.
added_claims.testable: yes - index series can be tested vs subsequent trend returns

added_claims.speaker: Niels
added_claims.quote: traders index up about 1% but still down 4%. Uh so far this year, MSEI World up 40 basis points in October as of last night
added_claims.claim: SG Short-Term Traders index was about +1% in October but about -4% YTD, much worse than the SG Trend index (+0.53% YTD) and the BTOP50 (+2.58%), i.e. faster-horizon CTAs lagged longer-horizon trend in 2025.
added_claims.indicator: SG Short-Term Traders index vs SG Trend index

added_claims.speaker: Rich
added_claims.quote: that's because liquidity is adaptive. It's not a static pool. It's seen to be like an elastic surface that moves and reforms with order flow.
added_claims.claim: Liquidity is adaptive, like an elastic surface: each trade consumes liquidity and signals direction, other traders react and quotes adjust, which is why impact is sublinear and the system is nonlinear.

added_claims.speaker: Rich
added_claims.quote: the verdict's out whether they are exactly fractal but certainly a fractal model has a better account and can understand why these situations occur
added_claims.claim: Caveat: Rich does not claim markets are exactly fractal; the fractal market hypothesis is only the closest available account of fat tails and power-law behaviour, not a definitive answer.
added_claims.testable: partly - tail exponents testable, model choice not decisive

added_claims.speaker: Rich
added_claims.quote: then there's um directionless volatility there's directional volatility um one might come with correlation might one might come without correlation
added_claims.claim: Volatility comes in directionless and directional forms, with or without cross-market correlation; this distinction (rather than a volatility level) is the signature of a live compress-and-expand fractal system.
added_claims.testable: yes - decomposable via trend vs noise measures

added_claims.speaker: Rich
added_claims.quote: I'm not using volatility measures to protect me or statistical measures because I think they're they're unsound.
added_claims.claim: Rich does not use volatility or other statistical risk measures to protect the portfolio because their assumptions come from a Gaussian world; protection comes from robust system design and sizing instead (the root of his disagreement with volatility-based sizing).
added_claims.testable: yes - compare drawdown with vol-scaled vs non-scaled sizing

added_claims.speaker: Rich
added_claims.quote: But on the hourly chart, those bursts at the micro level appear as clusters. Zoom out to the daily and a narrative forms.
added_claims.claim: Worked example of feedback cascading across scales (crude oil): tick-level buying ahead of a report, algorithms joining, hourly clusters, a daily narrative, then a monthly systemic move as producers, investors and policymakers reinforce it.

added_claims.speaker: Rich
added_claims.quote: Then selling accelerates, stops trigger, the system unwinds. Maybe even margin calls come into play, the system unwinds.
added_claims.claim: Reversal mechanics: once positive feedback breaks, selling accelerates, stop-losses trigger and margin calls force unwinding, so the energy stored in the trend is released quickly; Rich frames this as system renewal that restarts the cycle (reinforcement, alignment, reversal).
added_claims.indicator: trend reversals; stops and margin calls
added_claims.direction: sharp counter-trend moves after extended trends
added_claims.conditions: after valuation stretch and concentrated positioning
added_claims.testable: partly - reversal speed vs trend duration testable

added_claims.speaker: Niels
added_claims.quote: the risk of this Rich is that you are maybe less classic than than what what other what other trend followers might perceive as being classic
added_claims.claim: Caveat from Niels: mixing mean-reversion-into-trend and breakout systems in a behaviourally orthogonal ensemble makes Rich's approach less 'classic' trend following than what most allocators expect.

added_claims.speaker: Rich
added_claims.quote: We're not trying to forecast variance or optimize volatility. We're simply aligning our capital to the geometry of survival.
added_claims.claim: Closed-balance sizing aims at avoiding ruin rather than maximising return or targeting volatility; it embeds humility by sizing only from capital that has survived the realized path.
added_claims.testable: yes - compare terminal wealth and drawdowns under different sizing bases

added_claims.speaker: Niels
added_claims.quote: I'm thinking well there must be a reason why the majority at least of managers are not using that methodology.
added_claims.claim: Niels points out most managers use dynamic (volatility-based) sizing rather than closed-balance sizing, so the two are different design choices, not one right and one wrong; closed-balance sizing also lowers volatility.

added_claims.speaker: Niels
added_claims.quote: an easier way to build systems, to understand systems, maybe um maybe with less moving parts, but also a few discretionary parts
added_claims.claim: Niels concedes closed-balance, trade-by-trade sizing is simpler with fewer moving parts but contains discretionary elements (cutback rule), while dynamic sizing is more complex yet proven over 25-30 years of survival.

corrections.issue: Wrong speaker: the points that central banks succeeded in keeping inflation low and stable, and that the stability (not just level) of inflation drives the markets trend followers trade, are made by Niels (Rich only interjects 'kicked the can down low with compression').
corrections.fix: Niels: the stability of inflation, not just its level, strongly affects the markets trend followers trade; central banks succeeded in keeping inflation low and stable, which Rich links to the compression period.

completeness_estimate: 0.75 - first reader caught Rich's core framework (impact, reflexivity, non-ergodicity, fractals, closed-balance sizing, Niels' rebuttals); missed secondary mechanisms (adaptive liquidity, reversal mechanics, multi-scale cascade example, directional vs directionless volatility), several caveats/disagreement details, market-view items (energies, oil, dip-buying) and had one speaker error.
